+Some protocols derive several keys and IVs from a single KDF operation. TLS 1.2,
+for example, derives a key block that is split into client and server MAC keys,
+cipher keys and IVs. These functions let a provider perform such a derivation as
+one atomic operation and hand out the individual results afterwards. This is
+particularly relevant for providers backed by hardware or a token (for example
+PKCS#11), where the derivation produces key handles that are never exported as
+OSSL_FUNC_kdf_derive_multi() performs the derivation after processing the
+I<params> as per OSSL_FUNC_kdf_set_ctx_params(), deriving every key and IV at
+once and retaining them in the KDF context given by I<kctx>. A second call
+replaces the results of the first. Because they live in the context, they are
+released by OSSL_FUNC_kdf_freectx() and copied by OSSL_FUNC_kdf_dupctx(); a
+provider whose keys exist only as handles on a token and cannot be copied
+should fail the latter. The sizes and key types of the individual outputs are
+supplied as parameters, see L</KDF Parameters> below.
+Validating the requested sizes and types is the provider's job, and belongs
+here rather than at collection time: a provider whose keys live on a token has
+the whole template in hand at this point, so one the token refuses is rejected
+by the derivation itself.  The software providers do the same, checking a
+requested key length against the cipher that was named for it.
+The key type settled on for each purpose is reported through the ordinary
+OSSL_FUNC_kdf_get_ctx_params(), in a parameter named after the purpose. For
+a purpose the derivation produced no key for, the call should leave that
+parameter untouched and return success; libcrypto initializes each key-type
+parameter to an empty string before calling get_ctx_params(), and treats an
+empty result as indicating an absent key. This allows a caller to query the
+key types for several purposes in one call, some of which may be absent; a
+TLS 1.2 key block for an AEAD ciphersuite, for instance, has no MAC keys, but
+the query can still retrieve the cipher key type.
+OSSL_FUNC_kdf_get_skey() returns one of the keys, selected by the I<purpose>
+string; the recognised purpose strings are algorithm specific and are
+documented with the individual KDFs, for example in
+L<EVP_KDF-TLS1_PRF(7)> and L<EVP_KDF-TLS13_KDF(7)>. I<import> is the import
+function of the B<EVP_SKEYMGMT> that libcrypto resolved for this purpose from
+the key type reported above; a provider that already holds the key as a native
+object may ignore it and return that object instead. The caller takes ownership
+OSSL_FUNC_kdf_get_iv() returns one of the IVs, selected by the I<purpose>
+string. IVs are not keys and are handed back as raw bytes: on success I<*pIV>
+is set to point at the IV data and I<*pIVlen> to its length. That data remains
+owned by the KDF context and must stay valid until the context is reset, freed
+or used for another derivation; the caller must not free it.

+A named cipher also states the length of its own key, so "cipher_key_len" need
